summary: The developer machine has the core runtime, the documentdb MCP data-plane server, the Learn documentation server, and the full set of DocumentDB skills needed to implement the Python LangChain hybrid-search sample. Key facts the builder must change from the cold answers: full-text (BM25) uses createSearchIndexes + $search (not community $text as the primary path), vector indexes are created with createIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions (vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann), and the management/CLI surface is the az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster command groups and the documentdb az extension. Missing accelerators (local DocumentDB container) and missing small developer tools (mongosh) slow verification but have clear workarounds. Several cold answers described neighboring products (Cosmos DB RU-mode or older naming) and must be corrected before coding.
summary_points: All required agent skills (documentdb-*) and the documentdb MCP server are installed and available — the code build can start now.

Several cold answers are wrong or outdated about search (use $search + createSearchIndexes, not primarily $text), vector index creation syntax, connection-string shape (use mongodb+srv and mongocluster hostnames), and the CLI/ARM resource type names — the builder must follow the Microsoft Learn pages cited here.

Python (3.13 available), pip, node, npx, docker and git are present so sample code and local verification can run; mongosh is missing (useful for manual checks) but not blocking — add it or use the documentdb MCP server.
Local DocumentDB container is not running; running it would speed iterative index and query testing but is optional because a live cluster is provisioned and reachable.
Information gaps remain (embedding model + dims, sample dataset contents/license, top-N/fusion default values). These must be decided by the builder before index creation and seeding.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for accounts: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. (For the newer dedicated MongoDB-style clusters there is also Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The resource provider is Microsoft.DocumentDB and the dedicated cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (plural 'mongoClusters'); older Cosmos-account-style resources remain Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB accounts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and legacy Cosmos DB naming — the cold answer mixed the older databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB) resource and the newer dedicated cluster resource name and used 'mongodbClusters' instead of the documented 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the wrong ARM/Bicep resource type name or spelled it 'mongodbClusters', deployment templates or az CLI calls could fail or target the wrong resource family.
improvements: Update Azure CLI / templates docs to show the canonical resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' prominently on the quickstart and Bicep template pages.
Add a one-line mapping table in the 'What is Azure DocumentDB' overview that maps older Cosmos DB account types to the new mongoClusters resource name.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example commands: az cosmosdb create ... For dedicated MongoDB clusters use az cosmosdb mongodb cluster create -g MyRG -n myCluster ... (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension in normal installs.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The CLI exposes commands for mongo clusters under both 'az documentdb' (documentdb extension) and a 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' path in current docs; the official quickstart and command docs reference az documentdb / az documentdb mongocluster and also show az cosmosdb mongocluster in some command index pages. In practice the az extension 'documentdb' provides the cluster commands; Install or update the documentdb CLI extension if needed.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: CLI command groups have evolved: the documentdb extension exposes mongocluster commands and there are parallel az cosmosdb command pages; older docs or CLI defaults may cause ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the wrong CLI group or assumes the command exists in the core az install without the documentdb extension, CLI calls will error. The builder should ensure the documentdb CLI extension is present or use the explicit az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster commands shown in Learn.
improvements: Document the required az extension (documentdb) and the canonical command group in the quickstart and README.
In agent skill docs, prefer the 'az documentdb mongocluster' syntax and show the extension install command: az extension add --name documentdb --upgrade.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for MongoDB API accounts (and Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters for the dedicated MongoDB cluster resource where supported). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for MongoDB API accounts (and in newer azurerm versions there may be an azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongodb_cluster resource for dedicated clusters).
confusions.grounded_answer: For dedicated clusters use the Bicep/ARM resource Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (see templates docs). For CosmosDB account-style resources the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform examples and AzAPI providers provide 'mongoclusters' templates; check the provider version for the exact Terraform resource name (the Azure templates docs are authoritative for resource types).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the Bicep resource for Cosmos-account (`databaseAccounts`) and the newer dedicated mongoClusters resource and guessed Terraform names that depend on provider versions.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type in IaC would either fail to deploy or create the wrong kind of resource (Cosmos RU-mode account vs dedicated vCore cluster).
improvements: Add a short 'Which resource type to use' note in the Quickstart page that maps the typical IaC resource types (Bicep/ARM and the matching Terraform provider names) to the service variants (vCore cluster vs Cosmos RU account).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Standard MongoDB URI. Example for Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API): mongodb://username:password@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@. The host suffix is *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, TLS is required (ssl=true), port commonly 10255 for TLS endpoints, and options typically include replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB clusters you should generally use the SRV form: mongodb+srv://<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (or the global read-write endpoint *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com). The service provides distinct connection-string formats (SRV for cloud cluster endpoints). Older Cosmos DB Mongo API connection strings that use port 10255 and host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com describe the Cosmos DB (RU-mode) or older endpoints, not the dedicated DocumentDB cluster SRV hosts.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Enable private access in Azure DocumentDB (connection strings)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the older Cosmos DB-for-Mongo connection examples (port 10255, host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com) with the dedicated DocumentDB cluster SRV-style endpoints; both are MongoDB-compatible but have different hostnames and schemes.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong connection-string form (wrong host suffix or using a non-SRV URI) can produce connectivity failures, incorrect driver options, or accidentally target a different service variant.
improvements: In quickstarts and sample .env.example files, explicitly show the SRV-style connection string example for a cloud cluster and call out the older Cosmos DB (RU) 10255 form as legacy so builders don't copy the wrong pattern.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Two models: for Cosmos DB accounts (MongoDB API) throughput is billed as Request Units (RUs) provisioned at database/collection or using autoscale/serverless. For dedicated MongoDB-style clusters (the managed MongoDB-compatible 'cluster' SKUs) there are compute-tier instance sizes (vCore-like sizing, e.g. M-sizes such as M30) and disk-based billing. Expect RUs for CosmosDB accounts and vCore/instance tiers for dedicated MongoDB clusters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB (vCore/dedicated clusters) uses compute-tier instance sizes (M-sizes) and storage billing; Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU-mode) uses RUs. Use M-size tiers (M30 etc.) for vector-capable clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: None if builder picks the documented vCore tier specified in the run environment (M30).

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary data-plane auth for MongoDB API is MongoDB credentials (SCRAM username/password) and the TLS-based certificate options where supported. Management/control plane uses Azure AD (Microsoft Entra). There is not a generic MongoDB-wire-protocol mapping for Azure AD tokens in most drivers; drivers authenticate with the MongoDB username/password returned by the service. (If Azure AD integration is required for management, obtain an AAD token and use Azure management APIs.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: Azure DocumentDB supports both Native (SCRAM) credentials and Microsoft Entra ID authentication for data-plane (MONGODB-OIDC) when the cluster's auth modes include MicrosoftEntraID. The cluster can be configured to allow Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) auth, and drivers can connect using the OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism when provided with appropriate tokens. Management plane uses Azure AD as usual.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer assumed only SCRAM is supported for data-plane; newer cluster features explicitly add Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) modes for data-plane authentication.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID cannot be used for day-to-day connections, they might skip implementing role-based auth or OIDC support; conversely assuming OIDC is enabled when the cluster does not have it configured will cause auth failures.
improvements: Add a short 'Auth modes' note to the quickstart: show how to check cluster authAllowedModes and provide the sample connection string for both SCRAM and MONGODB-OIDC.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo or motor). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB driver — you use standard MongoDB client libraries pointed at the service URI. Azure provides azure-cosmos SDK for the SQL/Core API, but for MongoDB API use pymongo.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python). There is no separate special service-specific MongoDB binary driver; use pymongo or async motor, and use provider-specific helper libraries (langchain-azure-ai or langchain connectors) for vector integrations if desired.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: The cluster supports vector index types such as DiskANN, HNSW and IVF (as provided by the managed service). The creation is done with a MongoDB createIndex-style call for a vector field. Example (approximate) syntax: db.products.createIndex( { embedding: "knnVector" }, { name: "vec_idx", dimensions: 1536, metric: "cosine", indexType: "hnsw" } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds: vector-diskann, vector-hnsw and vector-ivf. Indexes are created via createIndexes or the server-side createIndexes command with a key mapping to 'cosmosSearch' and a 'cosmosSearchOptions' object specifying kind, dimensions, similarity and algorithm parameters (e.g., kind: 'vector-hnsw' or 'vector-diskann').

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer attempted to reuse community MongoDB knnVector syntax; Azure DocumentDB uses a cosmosSearch vector index form with cosmosSearchOptions in createIndexes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the wrong index-creation syntax the index creation will fail. Using knnVector-like syntax (community-only) would not create the DocumentDB vector index.
improvements: Replace any sample that shows 'knnVector' with the documented createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions template in the vector-search quickstart.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Basic full-text search uses MongoDB text indexes and the $text operator. For richer/hybrid search (text + vectors) you typically run two queries — a text search ($text) and a vector KNN search — then merge/scoring results in the application.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a new BM25-based full-text search preview that uses named search indexes created with createSearchIndexes and aggregation pipelines that begin with $search (e.g., $search + text/phrase/fuzzy). Hybrid search is implemented by running a BM25 $search against a search index and a vector cosmosSearch query and fusing the ranked lists (Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side $unionWith patterns). The community $text operator and text indexes still exist for basic text search, but the recommended path for ranked BM25 queries is createSearchIndexes + $search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the MongoDB community $text workflow rather than the DocumentDB preview full-text path (createSearchIndexes + $search) used for BM25 ranking.

confusion_sources.title: Full-text search and text indexes (Learn page acknowledging $text exists)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder implements BM25 using community $text indexes the results won't be BM25-ranked as DocumentDB's new FTS engine expects, and features like custom analyzers and fuzzy/phrase tuning won't be available.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Use $search for BM25' note in any overview quickstarts that still show $text, and update sample code to use createSearchIndexes + $search for ranked text retrieval.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Managed clusters typically advertise a supported MongoDB wire protocol/version (recent clusters can present as MongoDB 7.0). Expect most MongoDB 6.x/7.0 wire-protocol compatibility for drivers. Commonly-missing or limited features: some server-side admin commands, server-side JavaScript ($where), and a few engine-specific aggregation or transaction semantics may differ from upstream MongoDB; multi-document ACID behavior and some change stream semantics can be different or limited depending on the cluster SKU.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (per Learn docs). The service supports the vast majority of MongoDB operators (documentation states ~99.03% operator coverage). Some administrative or engine-specific commands and a small set of features may differ; builders should consult the MQL compatibility document for operator-by-operator support.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility table)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was directionally right about version compatibility but vague about which features are absent; the Learn compatibility pages are the authoritative source.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a specific unsupported admin command or feature is available could lead to runtime errors; the builder must check the compatibility docs for any advanced operator the sample might use.
improvements: Link to the MQL compatibility matrix in sample READMEs and encourage running the compatibility assessment when migrating.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For development use a local MongoDB Docker image matching the target wire version (e.g. mongo:7.0) and expose port 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists for SQL/Core APIs but does not fully emulate the MongoDB API/vector features; so prefer a local mongo container for local unit tests and use the live cluster for vector/index verification.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure provides a DocumentDB local gateway Docker image for local development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) that listens on port 10260; the quickstarts show starting that container and connecting with a connection string like mongodb://<admin>:<pass>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true. The Cosmos DB Emulator (SQL/Core) does not emulate the MongoDB/vector features; a plain mongo:7 container is a possible fallback for simple Mongo wire compatibility but it won't replicate DocumentDB's vector/search features. For vector/index verification use either the live cluster or the DocumentDB local container.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended mongo:7 as a fallback but omitted the DocumentDB local gateway image and the correct port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses a plain mongo container for vector/index testing they will not be able to exercise DocumentDB-specific vector engines or full-text preview features; tests may pass locally but fail or diverge when run against DocumentDB.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' note to quickstarts showing the DocumentDB local container image and the port (10260) so builders don't default to a plain mongo container.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: The service offers a change feed-like capability; some MongoDB change stream features are exposed depending on the cluster SKU and MongoDB API compatibility level. You may need a cluster configured with replica-set style behavior (the dedicated cluster SKU) to get full change-stream support. Expect to verify support on your cluster and possibly enable it in cluster settings.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams. Multi-shard change streams are available (preview) and may require enabling via the Features page or cluster preview settings. Change streams are resumable and support pre-images if configured on a collection. Verify and enable the relevant change-stream features (e.g., multi-shard change streams) in the cluster Features page if your workload requires them.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious and vague; the docs show change streams are supported and that some multishard functionality is a preview that must be enabled.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are not supported they might avoid implementing them even when available; if they assume multishard change streams exist by default they may miss an enablement step.
improvements: Add a quick 'enable change streams' snippet to the clustering and migration quickstarts describing where to toggle the preview feature.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The documentdb-specific MCP server (named documentdb in the environment) provides the data-plane inspection tools referenced by the sample. The general Azure MCP server covers resource management, but use the documentdb MCP server profile (documentdb/default) to run index inspection and query-plan commands against the cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server supplies data-plane tools for queries, aggregation, index management and query explanation; the general Azure MCP server covers control-plane and docs search.
confusions.grounding_source: machine_inventory (documentdb MCP present) and learn docs
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' was the original name for what became Azure Cosmos DB (the SQL API). The term 'DocumentDB' as used here maps to the Azure managed Cosmos DB service exposing a MongoDB-compatible API. This is unrelated to any separate open-source project named DocumentDB; Azure's DocumentDB became Cosmos DB and the MongoDB compatibility layer is an API surface on top of Cosmos DB (or on dedicated managed MongoDB-style clusters).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: The name landscape is confusing. The current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' was formerly called vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and was renamed to Azure DocumentDB. Separately, the original 'Azure DocumentDB' name was used historically (2014–2017) for the service that became Azure Cosmos DB. The current Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. It is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and from Cosmos DB RU-mode accounts.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple renames and the reuse of the 'DocumentDB' term across different eras led to conflation of the original DocumentDB->Cosmos renaming and the newer vCore-to-DocumentDB rename.
confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion in docs or sample text could lead builders to pick the wrong service/API (Cosmos RU-mode vs dedicated DocumentDB cluster) and create incompatible IaC or client options.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming timeline' table to the overview and quickstarts clarifying: original Azure DocumentDB (2014->Cosmos DB), Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) -> renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)', and note that Cosmos DB RU-mode remains separate.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the hood it's the Azure-managed storage/compute engine (Cosmos DB or a managed MongoDB cluster implementation) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol. That means application code can use standard MongoDB drivers, but some MongoDB server behaviors, admin commands, and advanced features may differ — test compatibility and indices. Use MongoDB drivers (pymongo) unchanged for CRUD and aggregation, but check feature parity for transactions, change streams and special commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation and MIT-licensed) and not by MongoDB server code; it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers with few changes, but builders must validate operator/command compatibility with the MQL compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer suggested 'Azure-managed engine' and conflated Cosmos DB engine vs DocumentDB open-source engine; docs specify the open-source DocumentDB engine powers the service.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the MongoDB server binaries are running under the hood, they might expect administrative commands or plugin behaviors that the DocumentDB engine doesn't implement; verify using the MQL compatibility docs.
improvements: Add a short 'Engine' paragraph in the overview that explicitly states the open-source DocumentDB engine underpins the service and links to the GitHub project.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector (KNN) index on the embedding field. Example (approximate): db.products.createIndex( { embedding: "knnVector" }, { name: "emb_vec_idx", dimensions: 1536, metric: "cosine", indexType: "hnsw" } ) — adjust indexType to DiskANN or IVF if you want those engines.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use createIndexes with a key that maps the vector path to 'cosmosSearch' and supply 'cosmosSearchOptions' specifying kind (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, or vector-diskann), dimensions, similarity (COS, L2, IP), and algorithmic params (efSearch/efConstruction/m, lBuild/lSearch/maxDegree, etc.). Example shown in the vector-search docs uses 'createIndexes' + 'cosmosSearchOptions'.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (create DiskANN/HNSW/IVF examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer attempted to reuse community MongoDB knnVector shape; DocumentDB uses cosmosSearch options in createIndexes.
confusions.build_risk: Index creation will fail if using the wrong syntax; vector index parameters (dimensions, kind) must match embedding model and cluster tier.
improvements: Provide a ready-to-copy createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions example in the sample repo README that matches the embedding dims used by the sample's chosen embedding model.

confusions.question: Which Python libraries will the sample use and how to install them?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo for DB access, sentence-transformers (or any embedding provider) for embeddings, and langchain for the agent. Install with pip: pip install pymongo sentence-transformers langchain openai (and any vector model client you plan to use).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use pymongo (or motor for async), a chosen embedding provider (OpenAI via openai or Azure OpenAI client, or sentence-transformers locally), and LangChain plus the Azure DocumentDB/azure-integrations (e.g., langchain-azure-ai or other connector libraries). The docs also recommend langchain-azure-ai or LlamaIndex integrations for vector stores. Pin exact versions in requirements.txt and document how to configure the embedding provider API key and DOCUMENTDB_URI in .env.

grounding_links.title: Use LangChain on Azure with Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer gave reasonable library choices but missed recommending the provider-specific LangChain connectors and the recommended pinned-package names used in Learn guidance.
confusions.build_risk: Using different connectors may require adapter code; embedding provider selection affects embedding dims and index parameters.
improvements: Supply a pinned requirements.txt in the sample repo with recommended packages (pymongo, langchain-azure-ai or llama-index connectors, openai or azure-openai client) and example .env.

confusions.question: How should the sample read and use the connection string in code?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient. Example: uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = pymongo.MongoClient(uri, tls=True); db = client['sample_retail_04']. Do not log or persist the raw URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (or similar env var), use the SRV-form URI if provided, ensure TLS is enabled, set recommended driver options (retryWrites=false, maxIdleTimeMS, authMechanism if using OIDC), and never persist secrets in code or logs. Use a .env.example and runtime env to store the connection string.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: None as long as TLS and recommended options are used and the secret is not logged.

confusions.question: How will the hybrid search be implemented in the sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Rewrite the user query to a search intent, compute an embedding, then run two searches: (1) a vector KNN aggregate using the vector index (e.g. a $search/$knn or createIndex + aggregate with knn stage) to get top-K by embedding similarity, and (2) a text search using a MongoDB text index ($text) or $search. Merge and re-rank results in the application by combining normalized vector and text scores, returning the top matches.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct idea, but implementation details must use DocumentDB's paths: use the prompt-engine rewrite + embedding, run a vector search via $search with the cosmosSearch vector operator against the vector index and run a BM25 text query via $search targeting a createSearchIndexes index (not community $text if you want BM25 features). Merge results using client-side RRF or server-side $unionWith/$group fusion as appropriate. Normalize scores because searchScore types are not directly comparable.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer recommended $text for BM25, whereas DocumentDB's BM25 path uses createSearchIndexes + $search; vector query should use cosmosSearch instead of guessed $knn stage.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses $text they will not get BM25-ranking or preview search features; merging scores from incompatible systems without normalization leads to poor ranking.
improvements: Provide a code snippet in the sample repo that runs both $search (BM25) and $search->cosmosSearch (vector) and demonstrates client-side RRF fusion with constants used in the sample.

confusions.question: What verification and inspection commands will the sample use via the documentdb MCP server?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile to inspect collections, indexes and query plans. Example commands (approximate): mcp documentdb inspect-collections --profile default --database sample_retail_04; mcp documentdb inspect-indexes --profile default --database sample_retail_04 --collection products; and mcp documentdb explain --profile default --database sample_retail_04 --collection products --pipeline '<aggregation-pipeline-json>'.
confusions.grounded_answer: The documentdb MCP server provides tools such as documentdb_list_databases (list DBs and collections), documentdb_list_indexes (list collection indexes), documentdb_explain_operation (explain a find/aggregate), documentdb_aggregate (run pipeline), documentdb_create_index (create index). Use those exact MCP tool names or equivalent CLI commands in scripts. The tool calls must pass connection_profile 'default' as the run environment expects.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory listing of tools)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer gave approximate 'mcp' CLI names rather than the exact MCP tool names present in inventory; the actual MCP tools are named documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.
confusions.build_risk: Using incorrect MCP command names in verification scripts will cause automation to fail; use the exact tool names from the inventory.
improvements: Document the exact MCP tool names and example calls in the sample README (e.g., documentdb_list_indexes --connection_profile default --db_name sample_retail_04 --collection products).

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and dimension
information_gaps.description: The prompt and skills don't pick a specific embedding provider/model (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, Azure OpenAI, or local sentence-transformers) nor the vector dimension to use. This affects vector index 'dimensions' and product-quantization settings. Looked in installed skills and Learn docs; they explain how to create vector indexes but do not prescribe an embedding model or dims for the sample.

information_gaps.title: Sample dataset source and size
information_gaps.description: No repository-provided sample dataset or license is included in the prompt or skills. The builder needs to know whether to generate synthetic data, use a public dataset, or rely on a provided seed. Skills mention 'load sample data' but none include an actual dataset or size guidance.

information_gaps.title: Default fusion/hyperparameter values
information_gaps.description: The prompt requests result fusion (hybrid search) but does not specify defaults (RRF k, fusion constant, top-N). The docs describe RRF and ranges but do not prescribe the values suitable for a 100-item demo vs a 100k catalog.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use createSearchIndexes + $search (BM25) for ranked full-text queries; do not rely on community $text as the primary BM25 path for DocumentDB full-text search.

Create vector indexes using createIndexes with a key mapped to 'cosmosSearch' and a 'cosmosSearchOptions' block specifying kind (vector-hnsw/vector-ivf/vector-diskann), dimensions and algorithm params — do not use community 'knnVector' syntax.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample: the build uses Python + the live cluster. If you want azd-style project templates add azd via its installer (see Azure Developer CLI docs).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample since the cluster is pre-provisioned and azure_writes_allowed=false; add if you plan to include Bicep IaC examples (install via 'az bicep install').

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for immediate sample build because the cluster is pre-provisioned; add only if the sample will include Terraform provisioning examples (install Terraform client).

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not needed for a Python LangChain sample; add only if you plan to provide .NET samples or run .NET quickstarts.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Worth adding for interactive, manual debugging of collections, indexes, and queries. Install mongosh from MongoDB's distribution or use your OS package manager. Alternatively use the documentdb MCP server's data-plane tools to run the same checks programmatically.
